title: Part 3: Inferential Statistics
text:
3.1 Three questions and three designs








Question
Dataset and observational unit
What supports the analysis?




How accurately can a sample estimate average order sales?
Superstore: one order
We explicitly draw a random sample from the fixed course frame


Do display conditions differ in mean weekly cola sales?
COLA: one store observed for one week
The book describes random assignment of 20 selected stores to two display conditions


How do household characteristics relate to card charges?
Consumer: one consumer record
An observational regression model; inference is conditional on model and sampling assumptions




Superstore is fictitious; its data do not establish facts about real retailers.
An independent row is a design assumption, not a property guaranteed by a spreadsheet.
COLA has different stores in its two columns; aligned rows are not pairs.
Consumer provenance does not establish random selection or causal effects.


# Each import cell locates data independently of YAML or earlier notebooks.
data_dir <- if (dir.exists("data")) "data" else file.path("..", "data")
source(file.path(data_dir, "..", "lessons", "_includes", "course-tools.R"))
lines <- read.csv(file.path(data_dir, "business", "superstore-lines.csv"),
                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE, colClasses = c(postal_code = "character"))
orders <- make_orders(lines)
cola <- read.csv(file.path(data_dir, "business", "cola.csv"))
consumer <- read.csv(file.path(data_dir, "business", "consumer.csv"))
knitr::kable(data.frame(data = c("Superstore orders", "COLA stores", "Consumer records"),
                       n = c(nrow(orders), nrow(cola), nrow(consumer))))

section: 3.2 Probability starts with a defined experiment
text:
3.2 Probability starts with a defined experiment
Experiment: Choose one of the 3,322 course-frame orders with equal probability.

Sample space: all course-frame order IDs.
Event RR: order ID appears in the source Returns table.
Event LL: recorded total order profit is negative.
0≤P(A)≤10\leq P(A)\leq1; P(S)=1P(S)=1; P(Ac)=1−P(A)P(A^c)=1-P(A).
For disjoint events, probabilities add.


probabilities <- orders %>% summarise(
  p_listed_return = mean(listed_return), p_loss_order = mean(loss_order),
  both = mean(listed_return & loss_order),
  either = mean(listed_return | loss_order))
knitr::kable(probabilities, digits = 4)




p_listed_return
p_loss_order
both
either




0.0575
0.202
0.0108
0.2486






These are exact proportions for the fixed frame, interpreted as probabilities under uniform random order selection.
“Not listed” means absent from the supplied Returns table; it does not independently verify that no return occurred.
Do not subtract presumed refunds from recorded profit; the workbook does not establish how returns enter the accounting fields.


Conditional probability and independence
P(R∣L)=P(R∩L)P(L),P(R∪L)=P(R)+P(L)−P(R∩L).P(R\mid L)=\frac{P(R\cap L)}{P(L)},\qquad
P(R\cup L)=P(R)+P(L)-P(R\cap L).

c(p_return = mean(orders$listed_return),
  p_return_given_loss = mean(orders$listed_return[orders$loss_order]),
  p_return_given_no_loss = mean(orders$listed_return[!orders$loss_order]))

              p_return    p_return_given_loss p_return_given_no_loss 
            0.05749548             0.05365127             0.05846850 



Conditioning changes the denominator.
Independence requires P(R∩L)=P(R)P(L)P(R\cap L)=P(R)P(L), or equivalent conditional relationships.
Different conditional rates in this frame describe an association, not a causal effect.



Reverse the conditioning with Bayes’ rule
P(L∣R)=P(R∣L)P(L)P(R).P(L\mid R)=\frac{P(R\mid L)P(L)}{P(R)}.

p_l <- mean(orders$loss_order)
p_r <- mean(orders$listed_return)
p_r_given_l <- mean(orders$listed_return[orders$loss_order])
c(direct = mean(orders$loss_order[orders$listed_return]),
  bayes = p_r_given_l * p_l / p_r)

   direct     bayes 
0.1884817 0.1884817 



The two answers agree because they use the same events and denominator definitions.
P(L∣R)P(L\mid R) and P(R∣L)P(R\mid L) answer different business questions.

title: Part 3: Inferential Statistics
text:
3.3 Random variables and distributions

A random variable assigns a number to the outcome of an experiment.
A discrete variable has countable values, such as the number of listed-return orders in a sample.
A continuous model describes values on a continuum, such as a model for measurement error.
For discrete XX, ∑xP(X=x)=1\sum_xP(X=x)=1 and E(X)=∑xxP(X=x)E(X)=\sum_x xP(X=x).
Var⁡(X)=E[(X−E(X))2]\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-E(X))^2] measures model variation.


Binomial: a model with stated assumptions
Model question: If ten independent future orders each had listed-return probability pp, what is the chance of at least one listed return?

Fixed number of trials; two outcomes per trial.
Independent trials; constant pp.
Using the historical frame proportion as pp is a model assumption, not a verified forecast.

X∼Binomial⁡(n,p),E(X)=np,Var⁡(X)=np(1−p).X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p),\quad E(X)=np,\quad
\operatorname{Var}(X)=np(1-p).

p <- mean(orders$listed_return)
c(p_at_least_one = 1 - pbinom(0, size = 10, prob = p),
  expected_count = 10 * p, count_sd = sqrt(10 * p * (1 - p)))

p_at_least_one expected_count       count_sd 
     0.4468609      0.5749548      0.7361369 

binomial <- data.frame(returns = 0:10, probability = dbinom(0:10, 10, p))
ggplot(binomial, aes(returns, probability)) +
  geom_col(fill = petra_ink) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10) +
  labs(x = "Listed returns among ten modelled orders", y = "Probability")










Hypergeometric: sampling the known frame without replacement
Different experiment: Randomly select ten distinct course-frame orders.

N <- nrow(orders)
K <- sum(orders$listed_return)
c(exact_without_replacement = 1 - dhyper(0, m = K, n = N - K, k = 10),
  binomial_approximation = 1 - dbinom(0, size = 10, prob = K / N))

exact_without_replacement    binomial_approximation 
                0.4473186                 0.4468609 



Hypergeometric probabilities account for sampling without replacement.
The binomial is close here because ten orders are a small fraction of the frame.
Sampling product lines instead would overweight orders containing many lines.



Poisson: counts over an exposure period

A Poisson model assumes independent events and a constant rate over the chosen exposure.
The following rate, three orders per hour, is an illustrative planning assumption.
It is not estimated from Superstore: the file has dates, not order times.


c(p_more_than_five = 1 - ppois(5, lambda = 3),
  mean_count = 3, variance_count = 3)

p_more_than_five       mean_count   variance_count 
      0.08391794       3.00000000       3.00000000 




Normal distributions and standardization
Z=X−μσ,Z∼N(0,1)when X∼N(μ,σ2).Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma},\qquad Z\sim N(0,1)
\quad\text{when }X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2).

c(p_within_two_sd = pnorm(2) - pnorm(-2),
  upper_975_percentile = qnorm(.975))

     p_within_two_sd upper_975_percentile 
           0.9544997            1.9599640 

normal_curve <- data.frame(z = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 300))
ggplot(normal_curve, aes(z, dnorm(z))) + geom_line(colour = petra_ink) +
  labs(x = "Standardized value z", y = "Density")









Area under the curve gives probability; height at a point is a density.
For a continuous model, P(X=x)=0P(X=x)=0 at any exact point.
Superstore order sales are strongly skewed; we do not assume the raw values are normal.

title: Part 3: Inferential Statistics
text:
3.4 Sampling distributions and standard errors

A parameter describes the target population or frame.
A statistic is calculated from a sample.
SD: variation between individual orders.
SE: variation of an estimator across repeated samples.
Under independent sampling, SE(x‾)≈s/nSE(\bar{x})\approx s/\sqrt{n}.
Without replacement from a finite frame, multiply by 1−n/N\sqrt{1-n/N} when using the sample variance with denominator n−1n-1.


Repeated sampling from Superstore

set.seed(307312)
n_sample <- 200
B <- 600
sample_means <- replicate(B, mean(sample(orders$sales, n_sample, replace = FALSE)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(frame_mean = mean(orders$sales),
  mean_of_sample_means = mean(sample_means),
  empirical_se = sd(sample_means),
  design_se = sd(orders$sales) / sqrt(n_sample) * sqrt(1 - n_sample / N)), digits = 2)




frame_mean
mean_of_sample_means
empirical_se
design_se




470.8
471.94
68.83
67.38




ggplot(data.frame(sample_mean = sample_means), aes(sample_mean)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = petra_ink, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(orders$sales), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Sample mean order sales ($), n = 200", y = "Samples")









The dashed line marks the known frame mean.
Sample means vary even though the source data do not change.
The central limit theorem concerns the sampling distribution of a mean, not normality of the raw data.
Severe skewness may require a large sample; “30 observations” is not a universal guarantee.
The randomization we perform supports inference to this fixed frame, despite repeated customers in the frame. It does not justify independent future-order models.

title: Part 3: Inferential Statistics
text:
3.5 Point and interval estimation
Question: Can a random sample estimate average sales across all course-frame orders?

set.seed(20261106)
sampled_orders <- orders[sample.int(N, n_sample, replace = FALSE), ]
xbar <- mean(sampled_orders$sales)
se <- sd(sampled_orders$sales) / sqrt(n_sample) * sqrt(1 - n_sample / N)
critical <- qt(.975, df = n_sample - 1)
mean_ci <- xbar + c(-1, 1) * critical * se
knitr::kable(data.frame(sample_n = n_sample, estimate = xbar,
  lower_95 = mean_ci[1], upper_95 = mean_ci[2], frame_mean = mean(orders$sales)), digits = 2)




sample_n
estimate
lower_95
upper_95
frame_mean




200
552.81
389.98
715.64
470.8






This is an approximate t interval with a finite-frame correction.
The target is the mean order sales in the fixed US, 2023–2025 course frame.
In repeated sampling, a 95% procedure aims to cover the fixed target about 95% of the time.
After the interval is computed, it either contains the target or it does not.
It does not mean that 95% of individual orders lie inside it.


See coverage rather than assume it

set.seed(907)
intervals <- replicate(600, {
  z <- sample(orders$sales, n_sample, replace = FALSE)
  half_width <- qt(.975, n_sample - 1) * sd(z) / sqrt(n_sample) * sqrt(1 - n_sample / N)
  mean(z) + c(-1, 1) * half_width
})
c(simulated_coverage = mean(intervals[1, ] <= mean(orders$sales) &
                              intervals[2, ] >= mean(orders$sales)),
  mean_interval_width = mean(intervals[2, ] - intervals[1, ]))

 simulated_coverage mean_interval_width 
          0.8833333         244.6788357 



Simulation results fluctuate; 600 runs do not establish the exact coverage probability.
In this seeded run, coverage is about 88%, materially below the nominal 95%. With this skewed frame, 200 orders are insufficient for reliable nominal t coverage.
This is a diagnostic counterexample: do not treat the nominal 95% label as validated precision. The full frame is available, so its exact mean is the primary descriptive answer.
Investigate a larger sample and compare empirical coverage before relying on this interval in a sampling project.
Increasing confidence widens an interval; increasing sample size usually narrows it.


# Compare the same approximate procedure at several sampling fractions.
coverage_by_size <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(200, 1000, 2000), function(n) {
  set.seed(907)
  bounds <- replicate(600, {
    z <- sample(orders$sales, n, replace = FALSE)
    h <- qt(.975, n - 1) * sd(z) / sqrt(n) * sqrt(1 - n / N)
    mean(z) + c(-1, 1) * h
  })
  data.frame(sample_n = n, fraction = n / N,
    empirical_coverage = mean(bounds[1, ] <= mean(orders$sales) &
                                bounds[2, ] >= mean(orders$sales)))
}))
knitr::kable(coverage_by_size, digits = 3)




sample_n
fraction
empirical_coverage




200
0.060
0.883


1000
0.301
0.933


2000
0.602
0.933






Larger samples improve coverage here, at a higher collection cost.
This is evidence about this frame and procedure, not a universal sample-size rule.



Estimate a proportion

return_interval <- prop.test(sum(sampled_orders$listed_return), n_sample,
                             conf.level = .95, correct = FALSE)
c(estimate = unname(return_interval$estimate),
  lower_95 = return_interval$conf.int[1], upper_95 = return_interval$conf.int[2],
  frame_proportion = mean(orders$listed_return))

        estimate         lower_95         upper_95 frame_proportion 
      0.06000000       0.03465219       0.10193169       0.05749548 



This score interval uses a binomial approximation and does not apply the finite-frame correction.
Our sample is about 6% of the frame; an exact without-replacement analysis would use the hypergeometric distribution.
The result describes the share listed in the Returns table, not a verified real-world return probability.


# An exact finite-frame alternative inverts the hypergeometric tails.
observed_returns <- sum(sampled_orders$listed_return)
possible_totals <- 0:N
compatible <- phyper(observed_returns - 1, possible_totals, N - possible_totals,
                       n_sample, lower.tail = FALSE) >= .025 &
              phyper(observed_returns, possible_totals, N - possible_totals,
                       n_sample) >= .025
range(possible_totals[compatible]) / N

[1] 0.03220951 0.10114389



These bounds concern the unknown fraction in a finite frame of 3,322 orders under simple random sampling without replacement.
Discreteness can make exact coverage conservative. We can check against the known full-frame fraction in this exercise.



Sample-size planning
For a large-population mean with a planning SD s0s_0 and desired margin EE:
n0≈(z.975s0E)2.n_0\approx\left(\frac{z_{.975}s_0}{E}\right)^2.

# A $100 margin is an illustrative management precision target.
E <- 100
s0 <- sd(orders$sales)
n0 <- (qnorm(.975) * s0 / E)^2
c(large_population_n = ceiling(n0),
  finite_frame_n = ceiling(n0 / (1 + (n0 - 1) / N)))

large_population_n     finite_frame_n 
               372                334 



This is a normal-approximation planning calculation, not a promise of realized precision.
Real projects need a defensible pilot SD, collection cost and sampling design.

title: Part 3: Inferential Statistics
section: 3.6 Hypothesis testing: start with the business claim
text:
3.6 Hypothesis testing: start with the business claim

Define the parameter, target and design.
State H0H_0 and H1H_1 before inspecting results.
Choose the significance level and test; check assumptions.
Calculate the effect, interval, test statistic and p-value.
State what the evidence supports and whether the effect matters.


Type I error: rejecting a true null; controlled at the chosen significance level under the test assumptions.
Type II error: failing to reject a false null.
Power: probability of rejecting a specified false null; depends on effect, noise, sample size and test.
A p-value is a probability of a result at least as extreme under the null model.
It is not the probability that the null is true or that a result occurred “by chance.”
Failure to reject is not proof of equality or equivalence.


A one-mean test with a stated benchmark
Planning question: Is mean weekly sales under the normal display different from 50 cases?

Fifty cases is a chosen planning benchmark, not a publisher-established target.
H0:μnormal=50H_0:\mu_{\mathrm{normal}}=50; H1:μnormal≠50H_1:\mu_{\mathrm{normal}}\ne50.
The following one-sample t analysis is model-based for comparable normal-display stores.
The 10 stores were not documented as a random sample of all supermarkets.


normal_sales <- cola$weekly_cases[cola$display == "Normal"]
t.test(normal_sales, mu = 50, alternative = "two.sided")


    One Sample t-test

data:  normal_sales
t = 0.05066, df = 9, p-value = 0.9607
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 50
95 percent confidence interval:
 36.90395 63.69605
sample estimates:
mean of x 
     50.3 



Use t when population SD is unknown and estimated from the sample.
A z test for a mean requires a defensibly known population SD or a justified large-sample approximation.
With ten observations, strong skewness or outliers would make ordinary t inference less secure.

title: Part 3: Inferential Statistics
text:
3.7 COLA: compare display conditions

The business experiment

Source: Berenson, Levine and Krehbiel, Basic Business Statistics, ninth edition, pp. 336–339.
Select 20 stores with similar storewide sales volume.
Randomly assign ten stores to normal shelving and ten to an end-aisle display.
Record cola sales during one week, in cases.
Each store contributes one observation. The course’s store IDs are labels added for convenience.

Question: How large is the mean difference, and is it distinguishable from zero?

cola_summary <- cola %>% group_by(display) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean_cases = mean(weekly_cases), sd_cases = sd(weekly_cases),
            median_cases = median(weekly_cases), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(cola_summary, digits = 2)




display
n
mean_cases
sd_cases
median_cases




End aisle
10
72.0
12.54
73.5


Normal
10
50.3
18.73
54.0




ggplot(cola, aes(display, weekly_cases, fill = display)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .4, alpha = .35, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = .06, height = 0, seed = 17), size = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = petra_display) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Weekly cola sales (cases)") + guides(fill = "none")










Welch two-sample t test
Let Δ=μend−μnormal\Delta=\mu_{\mathrm{end}}-\mu_{\mathrm{normal}}.
H0:Δ=0,H1:Δ≠0,t=x‾end−x‾normalsend2/nend+snormal2/nnormal.H_0:\Delta=0,\qquad H_1:\Delta\ne0,\qquad
 t=\frac{\bar{x}_{\mathrm{end}}-\bar{x}_{\mathrm{normal}}}
 {\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{end}}^2/n_{\mathrm{end}}+s_{\mathrm{normal}}^2/n_{\mathrm{normal}}}}.

end_sales <- cola$weekly_cases[cola$display == "End aisle"]
cola_test <- t.test(end_sales, normal_sales, alternative = "two.sided", var.equal = FALSE)
cola_test


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  end_sales and normal_sales
t = 3.0446, df = 15.723, p-value = 0.007849
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
  6.568701 36.831299
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y 
     72.0      50.3 



Mean difference: 21.7 additional cases per week, end aisle minus normal.
Approximate 95% interval: 6.57 to 36.83 cases.
Two-sided p-value: about 0.0078 under the Welch model.
At α=.05\alpha=.05, reject the zero-difference null under the stated assumptions.
The book uses a pooled-variance test; Welch avoids assuming equal population variances and gives slightly different results.
Random assignment supports a causal comparison within the experiment, subject to implementation and no interference between stores.
Generalizing to all stores or later weeks requires additional evidence.



Check assumptions and practical value

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
qqnorm(normal_sales, main = "Normal display"); qqline(normal_sales)
qqnorm(end_sales, main = "End-aisle display"); qqline(end_sales)




Normal Q–Q plots by display; ten stores per group provide limited diagnostic evidence.



par(mfrow = c(1, 1))


Check independence from the design, not a statistical normality test.
Inspect the distributions for unusual values and strong asymmetry.
A small-sample Q–Q plot cannot prove normality.
More sales are not automatically more profit: obtain contribution per case, display cost and displaced-product sales.
Do not invent these missing financial inputs.



When would a paired test be appropriate?

If the same stores were measured under both conditions, analyze within-store differences.
Account for period and carryover effects when planning such a design.
That is not the supplied COLA experiment, so do not use a paired test on these columns.


# Only for a genuinely paired design with matched observations:
# t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE)



More than two means

# A one-way ANOVA expresses the same two-group comparison with equal variances.
summary(aov(weekly_cases ~ display, data = cola))

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)   
display      1   2354    2354   9.269 0.00697 **
Residuals   18   4572     254                   
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



ANOVA compares group means; with more groups, a significant F test says at least one mean differs.
It does not identify which groups differ without planned contrasts or adjusted follow-up comparisons.
The classical model assumes independent errors, common error variance and suitable residual behavior.
We do not fabricate a third display condition to create an ANOVA dataset.

  sum(return_by_segment)

  fisher.test(return_by_segment)
} else {
  chisq.test(return_by_segment, correct = FALSE)
}
association_test


    Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data

data:  return_by_segment
p-value = 0.3822
alternative hypothesis: two.sided



Pearson’s chi-square test compares observed counts with counts expected under independence.
Inspect expected counts; this example uses Fisher’s exact test if any expected count is below five, otherwise Pearson’s chi-square approximation.
Here the random order sample supports a finite-frame exercise, with a small-sampling-fraction approximation.
This is not evidence about future retail customers, and repeated customers limit a future-order independence model.
Do not test all 6,682 lines as if they were independent customer responses.
Report conditional percentages and the size of differences alongside any p-value.
These examples are separate method demonstrations, not a preplanned confirmatory research program. Repeatedly searching for significant results inflates false positives.

3.9 Consumer: explain variation in credit-card charges

Business question and variables

Question: How are recorded card charges related to household income and household size?
Data: 50 records in Anderson’s Consumer.xls collection.
income_thousands: household income in thousands of dollars.
household_size: number of household members.
card_charges: recorded credit-card charges in dollars.
The workbook alone does not specify a reporting period; we do not add an annual label.
The source is a textbook case. Authenticity, representativeness and probability sampling are not independently established.

Yi=β0+β1Xi+εi.Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\varepsilon_i.

simple_model <- lm(card_charges ~ income_thousands, data = consumer)
summary(simple_model)

Response YY: card charges. Predictor XX: income in thousands of dollars.
Least squares chooses the line minimizing the sum of squared residuals.
A residual is observed minus fitted charges.
The slope is the estimated difference in mean charges associated with an additional $1,000 of income.
The intercept corresponds to zero income; this lies outside the observed income range and has limited business meaning.
The slope t test concerns H0:β1=0H_0:\beta_1=0 under the model assumptions.

\beta_2\text{household size}_i+\varepsilon_i.

summary(multiple_model)

Check the model

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

Residual patterns, normality, scale and influential observations for the multiple regression.



par(mfrow = c(1, 1))


Residuals versus fitted: look for curvature or changing spread.
Q–Q: assess whether normal-error inference is plausible.
Scale-location: look for unequal residual variation.
Leverage/Cook’s distance: investigate influential records without automatically deleting them.
Independence comes from collection design; residual plots cannot establish it.
Classical t/F intervals assume a suitable linear mean, independent errors and constant variance, with normal errors for exact small-sample inference.
If these assumptions are doubtful, treat the fit as descriptive or justify an alternative analysis before relying on p-values.



Confidence intervals versus prediction intervals
Profile: income of $45,000 and a three-person household, within the observed ranges.

profile <- data.frame(income_thousands = 45, household_size = 3)
predict(multiple_model, newdata = profile, interval = "confidence")

       fit      lwr      upr
1 3864.778 3746.969 3982.587

predict(multiple_model, newdata = profile, interval = "prediction")

       fit      lwr      upr
1 3864.778 3055.303 4674.252



Confidence interval: uncertainty about mean charges at that profile.
Prediction interval: uncertainty for one new comparable record; includes individual variation and is wider.
Neither is a causal estimate of what happens if a household’s income changes.
Avoid extrapolating beyond the observed income and household-size ranges.
A business deployment would need new-data validation and a defensible target population.

2.1 From a question to evidence

State the decision and the population or records of interest.
Identify the observational unit and relevant variables.
Check definitions, missingness and repeated records.
Summarize with a table, chart and numerical measures.
Explain the finding, limitations and next investigation.


Descriptive statistics: summarize the records you have.
Inferential statistics: use a sample or model to reason beyond observed records.
A large dataset does not automatically represent all retailers, customers or future years.


Import and establish the unit

data_dir <- if (dir.exists("data")) "data" else file.path("..", "data")
source(file.path(data_dir, "..", "lessons", "_includes", "course-tools.R"))
lines <- read.csv(file.path(data_dir, "business", "superstore-lines.csv"),
                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE, colClasses = c(postal_code = "character"))
orders <- make_orders(lines)
knitr::kable(data.frame(unit = c("Product line", "Order", "Customer"),
  records = c(nrow(lines), nrow(orders), n_distinct(lines$customer_id))))

3,322 orders: aggregate sales and profit by order_id.

A category can occur several times within an order; category line counts are not counts of customers.

title: Part 2: Descriptive Statistics
text:
2.2 Variables and measurement








Variable
Business meaning
Statistical treatment




order_id, customer_id, postal_code
Identify records, customers or places
Labels; arithmetic is meaningless


category, region, segment, ship_mode
Product, market and shipping classifications
Nominal categorical


quantity
Units sold on a line
Discrete numerical, ratio scale


sales
Recorded line sales in dollars
Numerical, ratio scale


profit
Recorded profit, including negative amounts
Numerical; avoid ratios of profits with arbitrary/negative bases


discount
Fractional discount, e.g. 0.20
Numerical; multiply by 100 for percent


order_date
Calendar date
Time; differences are meaningful


ship_days
Ship date minus order date
Discrete duration in days




Nominal: categories with no required ranking.
Ordinal: ordered categories without established equal spacing, such as satisfaction ratings.
Interval: equal differences, without an absolute zero, such as Celsius temperature.
Ratio: meaningful zero and ratios, such as units or elapsed time.
Superstore’s ship modes are service labels; the course does not assume an equal numerical spacing between them.


Sources and collection

Operational records capture transactions; surveys capture responses; experiments assign conditions.
A census covers every member of a defined frame; a sample covers a subset.
Probability sampling supports design-based inference when the sampling mechanism is known.
Convenience samples, nonresponse and coverage gaps may bias conclusions.
Superstore is fictitious. Its complete course extract is a finite teaching frame, not a sample of the real retail industry.



Check data before summarizing

          all(lines$discount >= 0 & lines$discount <= 1),

  labs(x = "Order sales ($)", y = "Orders")

title: Part 2: Descriptive Statistics
text:
2.5 Measures of central location
For observations x1,…,xnx_1,\ldots,x_n, the arithmetic mean is
x‾=1n∑i=1nxi.\bar{x}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i.

Mean: total divided by count; affected by unusually large values.
Median: middle ordered value, or the mean of the two middle values.
Mode: most frequent value/category; ties are possible.
For continuous amounts, exact-value modes often reflect rounding or repeated prices.


centre <- orders %>% summarise(orders = n(), mean_sales = mean(sales),

title: Part 2: Descriptive Statistics
text:
2.6 Spread and variation

Range: maximum minus minimum; depends only on two observations.
Mean absolute deviation from the mean: average absolute distance from the mean.
Sample variance: s2=∑(xi−x‾)2/(n−1)s^2=\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2/(n-1).
Sample standard deviation: s=s2s=\sqrt{s^2}, in the original units.
Frame variance: divide by NN when describing the entire fixed frame as a population.
IQR: third quartile minus first quartile; describes the middle 50%.

              sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2)), IQR(x)))

982.83


IQR
496.62






R’s var() and sd() use n−1n-1.
Variance has squared units; SD has dollar units here.
R’s mad() is a scaled median absolute deviation, not the mean absolute deviation above.
Variation across orders is not variation over time for an individual customer.


Coefficient of variation
CV=100sx‾.CV=100\frac{s}{\bar{x}}.

100 * sd(orders$sales) / mean(orders$sales)

[1] 208.7897



CV expresses SD relative to a positive mean on a meaningful ratio scale.
It can compare relative variation across positive measures with different scales.
Avoid CV for profit or margins that can be negative or have a mean near zero.
A high CV is descriptive; it does not by itself measure business risk.

title: Part 2: Descriptive Statistics
text:
2.7 Association between numerical variables
Question: Are larger orders necessarily more profitable?

ggplot(orders, aes(sales, profit)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#A3A3A3") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, colour = petra_ink) +
  labs(x = "Order sales ($)", y = "Order profit ($)")




Order-level sales and profit; large orders can also record large losses.





Covariance and Pearson correlation
sxy=∑i(xi−x‾)(yi−y‾)n−1,r=sxysxsy.s_{xy}=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{n-1},
\qquad r=\frac{s_{xy}}{s_xs_y}.

c(covariance = cov(orders$sales, orders$profit),
  pearson_r = cor(orders$sales, orders$profit),
  spearman_r = cor(orders$sales, orders$profit, method = "spearman"))

  covariance    pearson_r   spearman_r 
1.509486e+05 4.504704e-01 5.108097e-01 



Covariance has product units; its magnitude changes when units change.
Pearson rr is unitless and lies between −1 and +1 for nonconstant variables.
Pearson measures linear association; zero correlation does not imply no relationship.
Spearman correlation describes rank association and is a useful companion for skewed data.
Both can conceal group differences. Neither establishes causation.
Profit and sales are related accounting measures; a correlation is not an independent causal explanation.

title: Part 2: Descriptive Statistics
section: 2.8 Distribution shape, quartiles and unusual observations
text:
2.8 Distribution shape, quartiles and unusual observations

Right-skewed: long right tail; mean often exceeds median.
Left-skewed: long left tail; mean often falls below median.
Symmetry alone does not establish a normal distribution.
A numerical skewness index is useful alongside a histogram, not as a substitute.


c(mean = mean(x), median = median(x),
  pearson_second_skewness = 3 * (mean(x) - median(x)) / sd(x))

                   mean                  median pearson_second_skewness 
            470.7963893             153.9820000               0.9669055 

quantile(x, probs = c(0, .25, .5, .75, .9, .95, 1), type = 7)

        0%        25%        50%        75%        90%        95%       100% 
    0.8360    38.7150   153.9820   535.3375  1190.8090  1799.6705 23661.2280 



A percentile describes a position in the ordered distribution.
R’s default quantile(type = 7) interpolates between observations.
Different software conventions can give slightly different sample quartiles.


Boxplots and IQR fences

ggplot(orders, aes(segment, sales)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = petra_accent, outlier.alpha = 0.25) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Order sales ($)")




Order sales by customer segment; points beyond the whiskers are flags, not deletion instructions.



q <- quantile(x, c(.25, .75), type = 7)
fences <- c(lower = q[1] - 1.5 * IQR(x), upper = q[2] + 1.5 * IQR(x))
c(fences, flagged_orders = sum(x < fences[1] | x > fences[2]))

     lower.25%      upper.75% flagged_orders 
     -706.2188      1280.2713       301.0000 



Box: middle 50%; internal line: median.
Whiskers extend to the most extreme observations within the plotting fences.
Boxplot hinges can differ from the reported type-7 quartiles for some sample sizes.
Investigate flags for errors, genuine large transactions or a different business process.
Retain valid extremes. If useful, report a clearly labelled sensitivity analysis alongside the full result.



Standardized values

z <- (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)
c(min_z = min(z), max_z = max(z), beyond_3_sd = sum(abs(z) > 3))

      min_z       max_z beyond_3_sd 
 -0.4781004  23.5921053  53.0000000 



A z-score measures distance from the mean in SD units.
The familiar 68–95–99.7 rule applies approximately to normal distributions.
It is unsuitable as a blanket rule for skewed order values.

title: Part 2: Descriptive Statistics
text:
2.9 Put the evidence together
A useful management briefing contains:

Scope: US Superstore orders placed in 2023–2025; fictitious company.
Finding: Furniture has substantial sales but a thin recorded profit margin.
Evidence: category totals, weighted margins and the distribution of order values.
Interpretation: sales volume and profitability answer different questions.
Next step: examine subcategories, discount bands and large loss-making orders.
Limit: observed associations do not prove the effect of changing discounts.


Apply the methods

Practical 1: Product mix and categorical tables.
Practical 2: Order size and numerical measures.
Practical 3: Discounts, profitability and group comparisons.
Continue to Part 3 for uncertainty, tests and models.



Sources

Tableau Superstore sample data, downloaded 6 November 2026.
Tableau on dimensions, measures and transaction detail.
Course data dictionary and selection rules.
